root_cause.text: In `drivers/net/tap.c:tap_ioctl()`, the `SIOCGIFHWADDR` handler used an uninitialized on-stack `struct sockaddr_storage` that was only partially filled by `netif_get_mac_address()`, causing the remaining bytes copied via `ifr_hwaddr` to leak kernel stack data to userspace.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE/commit states that `tap_ioctl()` "copies 16 bytes of an uninitialised on-stack struct sockaddr_storage to userspace via ifr_hwaddr," while `netif_get_mac_address()` "only writes sa_family and dev->addr_len (6 for Ethernet) bytes, leaving sa_data[6..13] uninitialised"; the patch fixes this by changing `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` to `struct sockaddr_storage ss = {};`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Zero-initialize the local sockaddr_storage in tap_ioctl() to avoid using uninitialized stack data.
intent_record.what: In tap_ioctl(), the declaration of the local variable `ss` was changed from `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` to `struct sockaddr_storage ss = {};`, and its position was moved slightly earlier among the local variable declarations.
intent_record.how: This zero-initializes the entire `sockaddr_storage` object before any later use, preventing reads of uninitialized stack contents and ensuring any fields not explicitly set start in a known zero state at runtime.

grouping_result.intent: Zero-initialize the local sockaddr_storage in tap_ioctl() to avoid using uninitialized stack data.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly fixes the root cause by zero-initializing the on-stack sockaddr_storage in tap_ioctl(), preventing uninitialized stack bytes from being exposed through SIOCGIFHWADDR.

candidates.rationale: This stack variable is declared without initialization. Because the SIOCGIFHWADDR path only partially fills it via netif_get_mac_address(), later copying out ifr_hwaddr can expose uninitialized bytes from the kernel stack to userspace.

vuln_statements.explanation: This on-stack sockaddr_storage was declared without initialization in tap_ioctl(). In the SIOCGIFHWADDR path, netif_get_mac_address() only populated part of the structure, so later copying ifr_hwaddr to userspace could include leftover uninitialized stack bytes, causing an information leak.

bic_trace_step.reason: The diff shows the exact SIOCGIFHWADDR handling in tap_ioctl() and is sufficient to judge the issue. The root cause was use of an uninitialized on-stack object that was only partially filled, then copied to userspace. In this commit, the old vulnerable pattern using `struct sockaddr sa;` and `copy_to_user(&ifr->ifr_hwaddr, &sa, sizeof(sa))` is gone. It has been replaced with `struct sockaddr_storage ss;` and `dev_get_mac_address((struct sockaddr *)&ss, ...)`, followed by `copy_to_user(&ifr->ifr_hwaddr, &ss, sizeof(ifr->ifr_hwaddr))`. This matches the fix pattern for avoiding the partial-copy leak from the smaller/incorrect stack object. Additionally, the SIOCSIFHWADDR path was updated to use `struct sockaddr_storage ss` and includes a new bounds check `if (tap->dev->addr_len > sizeof(ifr->ifr_hwaddr)) ret = -EINVAL;`, which is further evidence this commit contains the corrective handling. Therefore the vulnerable construct is absent in this version, and the fix is present.
